summary: Describes where and how the Label Distribution Protocol is meant to be used in MPLS networks. It explains the situations LDP suits, rather than defining new protocol rules. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: LDP is one way for MPLS routers to tell neighbors what a label means. RFC 3037 describes where LDP is useful and how its operating choices affect label use and scaling.

subtitle: Where LDP fits among the ways MPLS routers can distribute labels.

tldr.problem: MPLS routers need a shared understanding of what labels mean. Different label-distribution methods suit different forwarding and resource conditions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes LDP for normally routed, hop-by-hop paths and outlines its sessions, distribution modes, retention choices, loop detection and extension mechanism.
tldr.outcome: It recommends LDP implementation for devices that perform MPLS forwarding along normally routed paths. Explicitly routed traffic-engineering paths may use CR-LDP or RSVP-TE.

facts.label: Label distribution methods
facts.value: Downstream Unsolicited and Downstream on Demand

today: RFC 3037 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: LDP and Normally Routed Paths
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching forwards packets using short, fixed-length labels. Neighboring Label Switching Routers (LSRs) must agree on what each label means; a label-distribution protocol communicates those bindings.

LDP is designed to distribute labels for MPLS forwarding along paths selected by destination-based routing. The memo calls this hop-by-hop forwarding and recommends LDP for devices that perform it.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use labels to forward packets, but each router must know what its neighbor's label means. LDP carries that information for ordinary routed paths.

sections.title: Where LDP Is Useful
sections.content:
LDP can work with an IP routing plane and software that programs ATM or Frame Relay switch tables. This can carry IP over those switched networks without an overlay or their native addressing and routing.

The memo also identifies hop-by-hop routed tunnels, including MPLS-based VPNs and tunnels between BGP border routers. LDP does not rely on every node supporting the same label-distribution method piggybacked on a routing protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: LDP can distribute labels across networks built from different kinds of equipment. It can also support routed tunnels where the path follows normal routing.

sections.title: Sessions and Label Distribution Choices
sections.content:
LDP associates a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) with each label. Peers establish an LDP session over TCP, which reliably delivers session messages. A discovery mechanism can find potential peers without configuring each one manually.

With Downstream Unsolicited distribution, an LSR advertises a binding when ready to forward the FEC. With Downstream on Demand, it sends a binding after a peer requests one. Liberal retention keeps learned labels even when not currently needed; conservative retention keeps only labels in immediate use.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can advertise labels when ready or provide them only when asked. They can also keep all labels they learn or keep only the ones they currently need.

sections.title: Choosing Modes for Scale
sections.content:
When labels are scarce, such as on ATM and Frame Relay links, the memo says Downstream on Demand with conservative retention can conserve labels. When labels are plentiful, Downstream Unsolicited with liberal retention can make a next-hop change require no new label-distribution action.

LDP distribution is incremental and does not need periodic binding refreshes. More TCP connections limit the number of peers an LSR can support, and path-vector loop detection uses extra memory, processing and protocol traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: If labels are scarce, routers can request and keep only needed labels. If labels are plentiful, keeping more labels can make route changes easier.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering and Security
sections.content:
Traffic engineering uses explicitly routed Label Switched Paths that need not follow normal routes. The memo identifies CR-LDP and RSVP-TE as ways to set up such paths and makes no recommendation about which is technically superior.

LDP optionally uses the TCP MD5 Signature Option to protect session connections against injected spoofed TCP segments. The loop-detection mechanism may be disabled by configuration, but a compliant LSR must implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: For a path chosen for traffic engineering, the memo leaves the choice between CR-LDP and RSVP-TE to administrators. LDP can also use TCP MD5 protection for its sessions.
